title: Understanding Student Interaction with AI-Powered Next-Step Hints: Strategies and Challenges
venue: Proceedings of the 57th ACM Technical Symposium on Computer Science Education V.1 (SIGCSE TS 2026)
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how students interact with an AI-powered next-step hint system for programming tasks, with a particular focus on two questions: what behavioral patterns appear in student hint use, and what strategies students use when hints are unhelpful. The authors argue that while prior work has evaluated automated feedback quality, less is known about how learners actually engage with such hints during problem solving, especially in in-IDE learning environments.

The intervention studied is an AI-based next-step hint system integrated into the JetBrains Academy plugin for learning Kotlin inside a professional IDE. The system provides two levels of support: a textual hint that suggests one actionable next step, and a code hint that shows a code fragment to move the solution forward. The study combines quantitative log analysis and qualitative interviews. Using detailed KOALA logs, the authors analyzed hint-request sessions from students' task-solving processes and applied process mining to identify 16 common interaction scenarios. They also conducted semi-structured interviews to better understand how students responded to ambiguous or unhelpful hints.

The population consisted of 34 first- and second-year computer science Bachelor's students with prior programming experience in languages other than Kotlin but no prior Kotlin experience. Students completed three Kotlin programming projects from a JetBrains Academy onboarding course in an in-IDE environment; 20 completed all three projects, and 6 of those students participated in 30-minute interviews. The context was programming education using JetBrains IDEs and an AI hint tool, with an expected total task completion time of up to six hours.

The main findings are that student interactions with the hint system were varied: 28.48% of scenarios were positive, 40.00% were neutral, and 27.05% were negative, with most negative cases caused by system errors rather than explicit rejection. Interviews and log inspection showed that students often used hints strategically rather than passively. They selectively adapted only parts of code hints, or requested multiple hints and combined partial suggestions to build a working solution. The authors conclude that students can engage with AI hints in flexible and sometimes unexpected ways, and that hint systems should better support these behaviors, for example by improving robustness and potentially offering multiple hint variations.

identified_tools.name: JetBrains Academy plugin
identified_tools.description: An in-IDE learning plugin for JetBrains IDEs that integrates programming tasks and AI-based next-step hints, including textual and code hints generated using LLMs combined with static analysis.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as the environment hosting an AI-powered next-step hint system for students solving Kotlin programming tasks; the paper analyzed log data and interviews to understand how students interacted with textual and code hints and how they handled unhelpful hints.

findings.finding_summary: Across hint-request scenarios from 34 students solving Kotlin tasks, 28.48% of interactions were positive (299 scenarios), 40.00% were neutral (420 scenarios), and 27.05% were negative (284 scenarios). Most negative scenarios were due to internal system errors rather than explicit rejection, and the authors note that students often continued using the system after encountering such errors.
findings.measure: Distribution of hint interaction scenarios (positive, neutral, negative) derived from log data

findings.finding_summary: The log dataset included 960 textual hint requests and 453 code hint requests, and process mining identified 16 common interaction scenarios. Positive and neutral scenarios together accounted for 68.48% of all scenarios, suggesting students frequently engaged with the hint system without explicitly rejecting hints.
findings.measure: Hint request counts and process-mined interaction scenario frequencies

findings.finding_summary: Semi-structured interviews with 6 students identified strategies for handling unhelpful hints, including selective use of hints and combining partial solutions from multiple hints. Manual analysis showed some students adapted only parts of code hints, generated multiple hint variants by changing code, and combined these variants into working solutions.
findings.measure: Student problem-solving and hint-use strategies from interviews and follow-up log analysis

findings.finding_summary: Most negative hint interactions were attributable to system errors: 266 out of 284 negative scenarios resulted from internet connection problems or internal issues involving LLM providers and access tokens. Process mining also showed ERR → HBC was relatively common, accounting for an average of 9.8% of all transitions, indicating students often returned to request hints after errors.
findings.measure: System error frequency and transition behavior after errors

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-methods study with detailed log analysis and interviews, but it does not use an RCT or quasi-experimental design and focuses on interaction patterns rather than causal learning effects.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper provides useful evidence on student interaction patterns and system usability, but it does not report standardized effect sizes or direct achievement gains, so impact on learning outcomes remains unclear.
